sections.heading: 3.1 How Cells Are Studied

blocks.text: A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing. A living thing, like you, is called an organism. Thus, cells are the basic building blocks of all organisms.

In multicellular organisms, several cells of one particular kind interconnect with each other and perform shared functions to form tissues (for example, muscle tissue, connective tissue, and nervous tissue), several tissues combine to form an organ (for example, stomach, heart, or brain), and several organs make up an organ system (such as the digestive system, circulatory system, or nervous system). Several systems functioning together form an organism (such as an elephant, for example).

There are many types of cells, and all are grouped into one of two broad categories: prokaryotic and eukaryotic. Animal cells, plant cells, fungal cells, and protist cells are classified as eukaryotic, whereas bacteria and archaea cells are classified as prokaryotic. Before discussing the criteria for determining whether a cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic, let us first examine how biologists study cells.

sections.heading: Microscopy

blocks.text: Cells vary in size. With few exceptions, individual cells are too small to be seen with the naked eye, so scientists use microscopes to study them. A microscope is an instrument that magnifies an object. Most images of cells are taken with a microscope and are called micrographs.

To give you a sense of the size of a cell, a typical human red blood cell is about eight millionths of a meter or eight micrometers (abbreviated as µm) in diameter; the head of a pin is about two thousandths of a meter (millimeters, or mm) in diameter. That means that approximately 250 red blood cells could fit on the head of a pin.

The optics of the lenses of a light microscope changes the orientation of the image. A specimen that is right-side up and facing right on the microscope slide will appear upside-down and facing left when viewed through a microscope, and vice versa. Similarly, if the slide is moved left while looking through the microscope, it will appear to move right, and if moved down, it will seem to move up. This occurs because microscopes use two sets of lenses to magnify the image. Due to the manner in which light travels through the lenses, this system of lenses produces an inverted image (binoculars and a dissecting microscope work in a similar manner, but include an additional magnification system that makes the final image appear to be upright).

All cells fall into two broad categories. These categories are prokaryotic and eukaryotic. Animal cells are eukaryotic. Plant cells are eukaryotic. Fungal cells are eukaryotic. Protist cells are eukaryotic. Bacteria cells are prokaryotic. Archaea cells are prokaryotic. We will look at how biologists study cells first.

repaired_sections.heading: 3.1 How Cells Are Studied
repaired_sections.text: A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing. A living thing, like you, is called an organism. Cells are the basic building blocks of all organisms. In multicellular organisms, cells of one kind connect. They share functions to form tissues. Examples include muscle tissue, connective tissue, and nervous tissue. Several tissues combine to form an organ. Examples are the stomach, heart, or brain. Several organs make up an organ system. Examples are the digestive system, circulatory system, or nervous system. Several systems working together form an organism. An example is an elephant. There are many types of cells. They fall into two broad categories: prokaryotic and eukaryotic. Animal cells, plant cells, fungal cells, and protist cells are eukaryotic. Bacteria and archaea cells are prokaryotic. Before we look at how to tell them apart, let us see how biologists study cells.

repaired_sections.heading: Microscopy
repaired_sections.text: Cells vary in size. Most cells are too small to see with the naked eye. Scientists use microscopes to study them. A microscope is an instrument that magnifies an object. Most images of cells are taken with a microscope. These images are called micrographs. A typical human red blood cell is about eight millionths of a meter. This is eight micrometers (abbreviated as µm) in diameter. The head of a pin is about two thousandths of a meter. This is millimeters, or mm, in diameter. Approximately 250 red blood cells could fit on the head of a pin. The lenses of a light microscope change the image orientation. A specimen right-side up and facing right on the slide looks upside-down and facing left. This happens when viewed through a microscope. If you move the slide left, it appears to move right. If you move it down, it seems to move up. This occurs because microscopes use two sets of lenses. Light travels through these lenses in a specific way. This system produces an inverted image. Binoculars and a dissecting microscope work similarly. They include an extra magnification system. This makes the final image appear upright.
